title: Metadata-Driven Architecture on Fabric
purpose: Show how a versioned metadata contract drives a single reusable Data Factory pipeline and reusable notebooks, and how run state feeds back into the next run instead of being thrown away.
accessibleSummary: A metadata contract describing sources and load rules is resolved into per-object configuration, which a single reusable Data Factory pipeline and reusable notebooks execute against Fabric compute. Each run writes data into a lakehouse and records state, quality, and lineage telemetry in a run ledger; the ledger both proves what happened and supplies the watermark the next run reads to stay restartable. Two warning nodes call out where this pattern breaks: an over-grown metadata schema that turns into an untyped programming language, and non-idempotent writes that corrupt data on retry.
longDescription: This diagram traces one execution of a metadata-driven load on Microsoft Fabric. A versioned metadata contract (object list, source connection, target shape, quality rules, load type) is resolved at run start into a concrete parameter set for one data object. That resolved configuration parameterizes a single reusable Data Factory pipeline, which invokes a reusable notebook for object-agnostic transform logic rather than one pipeline and one notebook per source. Execution lands data in a lakehouse via managed Delta tables. Every run — success or failure — writes to a run ledger that records status, rows processed, and the watermark for the next run; that ledger is what makes the framework restartable, and it feeds back into config resolution for the following run (the feedback edge). Quality checks evaluate the landed data against the contract's rules and post evidence forward; lineage and telemetry are captured for governance and observability. Two warning nodes are deliberately included: the metadata contract can accrete conditional logic until it functions as an undocumented programming language understood by no single person, and a non-idempotent pipeline write will corrupt or duplicate data if a failed run is blindly retried without the ledger's watermark discipline.

nodes.label: Versioned metadata contract
nodes.summary: Object list, source, target shape, quality rules, load type — versioned like code.
nodes.detail: A structured, version-controlled record (table, file, or config store) listing every data object the framework loads: its source connection, target Fabric item, column/type expectations, quality rules, load type (full vs incremental), and ownership. Because it is versioned, a schema or rule change is auditable and reversible, the same discipline applied to claims in this knowledge base.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the single place that defines what 'correct' looks like for every object. If it drifts silently, every downstream run inherits the drift with no record of why.

inputs: Source system inventory
Business rules from data owners
Prior contract version
processing: Author or edit one row/entry per data object
Validate the new version against a schema (required fields, allowed load types)
Commit as a new version; tag the prior version as superseded
outputs: Machine-readable contract consumed by config resolution
Change history for audit
drill.example: A new source table 'returns' is added to the contract with load_type=incremental, watermark_column=updated_at, and a not-null rule on order_id; the contract version increments from v14 to v15.
controls: Who can approve a new contract version
Required-field schema for a contract entry
Whether breaking changes require a review gate
failureModes: Contract accretes per-object exceptions and conditional flags until reading it requires reading code, not config
A contract change ships without versioning, so a bad edit cannot be diffed or rolled back
Two teams edit the same object entry concurrently and one change is silently lost

nodes.label: Config resolution
nodes.summary: Turns the generic contract into one object's concrete run parameters.
nodes.detail: At run start, this step reads the metadata contract plus the current watermark from the run ledger and resolves them into the concrete parameter set for a single object: which connection to open, which incremental window to pull, which target table to write, and which quality rules apply. This is the translation layer between declarative metadata and an executable run.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is where 'metadata' actually becomes 'a run' — if resolution logic is wrong, every object it touches gets the wrong parameters, not just one.

inputs: Metadata contract (current version)
Last successful watermark from run ledger
Trigger context (schedule or event)
processing: Look up the object's contract entry
Read the last committed watermark for that object from the ledger
Build the concrete parameter payload (connection, window, target, rules) for this run
outputs: Resolved parameter set handed to the pipeline invocation
drill.example: For 'returns', resolution reads last watermark updated_at=2026-07-11T00:00Z from the ledger and produces parameters: window=[2026-07-11T00:00Z, now], target=lh_bronze.returns, rules=[not_null(order_id)].
controls: Resolution logic itself (code, not data) — kept intentionally thin
Fallback behavior when no prior watermark exists (first run)
failureModes: Resolution silently defaults a missing contract field instead of failing the run, masking a bad contract entry
Clock or timezone mismatch between the watermark and the source system skips or duplicates a window of rows

nodes.label: Reusable Data Factory pipeline
nodes.summary: One parameterized Data Factory pipeline drives every object instead of one pipeline per source.
nodes.detail: A single generic Data Factory pipeline accepts the resolved parameter set and executes the movement/orchestration steps common to every object: connect, copy or trigger transform, checkpoint. Fabric pipelines are the orchestration layer that chains data movement and transformation activities with control-flow constructs, authored once and driven by parameters rather than duplicated per source.
nodes.whyItMatters: Reuse is what keeps the framework's maintenance cost flat as object count grows — the alternative is one pipeline per source, which is the config-explosion problem this pattern exists to avoid.

evidence.note: Data Factory is Fabric's data integration workload: it connects to data sources, moves data, transforms it, and orchestrates movement and transformation tasks from a single place.

inputs: Resolved parameter set from config resolution
processing: Bind incoming parameters to pipeline variables
Execute copy/transform activities using those variables instead of hard-coded values
Invoke the reusable notebook for object-specific transform logic
Emit a run status signal on completion or failure
outputs: Triggered notebook execution
Run status event to the run ledger
drill.example: The pipeline binds source_connection, target_table, and window parameters for 'returns', runs a Copy activity into the bronze zone, then calls the reusable transform notebook.
controls: Pipeline parameter schema
Retry policy per activity
Concurrency/parallelism settings for the pipeline
failureModes: A parameter name typo between config resolution and the pipeline is silently ignored at run time and the pipeline falls back to a default instead of erroring
An activity retry re-runs a non-idempotent write and duplicates rows already committed on a prior attempt

nodes.label: Pipeline run instance
nodes.summary: Each trigger produces one concrete, individually monitorable run.
nodes.detail: A pipeline run is one execution instance of the pipeline, started on demand, on a time-based schedule, or from an event trigger such as a file arriving in storage. Each run is tracked independently, which is what lets the framework retry or inspect one failed object without touching the others.
nodes.whyItMatters: Treating each object's execution as its own run instance, rather than one big batch job, is what makes per-object retry and monitoring possible at all.

evidence.note: A pipeline run is one execution instance of a pipeline and can be started on demand, on a schedule, or from an event trigger such as files arriving in storage.

inputs: Trigger signal (schedule, event, or manual)
Pipeline definition + bound parameters
processing: Fabric allocates a run ID and starts activity execution
Activities execute in the order/branches defined by the pipeline
Run status (succeeded/failed/in progress) is tracked for this run ID
outputs: Activity outputs (copied/transformed data)
A run ID and status usable for monitoring and retry
drill.example: An event trigger fires when a new file lands for 'returns'; Fabric starts run ID 8472 and tracks its activities independently of any other object's concurrent run.
controls: Trigger type (schedule vs event vs manual)
Per-run timeout and retry count
failureModes: Manual test runs never generate scheduled-run failure notifications, so a person watching only email alerts misses failures from manual runs
Two triggers overlap for the same object and their runs race on the same target table

nodes.label: Reusable notebook transform
nodes.summary: Object-agnostic transform logic runs once per object, parameterized the same way as the pipeline.
nodes.detail: The pipeline invokes one shared notebook that performs the transform logic common to every object — the notebook itself has no per-source branching hard-coded into it; it reads its behavior from the same parameter set the pipeline was resolved with. This keeps transform logic in one auditable place instead of scattered across a copy-pasted notebook per source.
nodes.whyItMatters: A per-source notebook copy is the same config-explosion failure as a per-source pipeline, just moved one layer down — this node is where that risk gets reintroduced if the reuse discipline slips.

inputs: Bound parameters from the pipeline invocation (object, window, target)
Landed or in-flight source data for the current run
processing: Notebook reads its run parameters instead of a hard-coded object name
Applies the same transform steps regardless of which object is running
Hands transformed rows to the Delta write step
outputs: Transformed rows ready to land in the lakehouse
Notebook execution status returned to the pipeline
drill.example: The shared notebook receives object=returns and window=[2026-07-11T00:00Z, now], applies the standard bronze-to-silver cleansing steps, and writes the result — the same notebook ran for 'orders' an hour earlier with different parameters.
controls: Notebook parameter cell/widget definitions
Compute pool/session sizing for the notebook run
failureModes: A one-off object exception gets hard-coded into the notebook with an if-branch instead of a contract field, reintroducing per-source logic sprawl
Notebook session cold-start latency is charged to every small object equally, even ones that would run faster as a lighter-weight activity

nodes.label: Lakehouse landing (Delta)
nodes.summary: Data lands as managed Delta tables, auto-registered and immediately queryable.
nodes.detail: The pipeline/notebook writes the object's data into a Fabric lakehouse's managed Tables area. Fabric validates the Delta format, extracts schema and partitioning metadata, and registers the table in the metastore automatically, so it is queryable from Spark or T-SQL without a manual CREATE TABLE step.
nodes.whyItMatters: Auto-registration removes an entire class of manual schema-drift bugs that plague hand-rolled loaders, but it also means a bad write is immediately visible to every consumer — there is no staging gate unless the framework adds one.

evidence.note: When data lands in the managed Tables area, Fabric validates the Delta format, extracts schema/partitioning metadata, and registers the table in the metastore, making it immediately queryable from Spark SQL or T-SQL.

inputs: Transformed rows from the notebook step
Target table path from resolved config
processing: Write rows as Delta files to the target Tables path
Fabric validates the Delta format and extracts column/type/partition metadata
Table is registered in the metastore for Spark SQL / T-SQL access
outputs: Queryable managed Delta table
Updated table metadata for the metastore
drill.example: 'returns' rows are written to Tables/bronze/returns as Delta; the metastore registers the table with its inferred schema, and it is immediately queryable via the SQL analytics endpoint.
controls: Write mode (append/merge/overwrite) chosen per load_type in the contract
Target zone (bronze/silver/gold) selection
failureModes: A retry after partial failure re-appends already-written rows because the write is append-only and not idempotent
Only Delta format is supported for metastore auto-registration; a non-Delta write silently fails to register

nodes.label: Quality evidence
nodes.summary: Contract-defined rules are evaluated against the landed data and recorded as evidence.
nodes.detail: The quality rules declared per object in the metadata contract (not-null checks, row-count thresholds, referential checks) are evaluated against the data that just landed. The result — pass, fail, or a specific rule violation — is recorded as evidence attached to that run, not just logged and discarded.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without recorded evidence, 'the load succeeded' and 'the load produced correct data' are conflated; this node is what keeps them separate and auditable.

inputs: Landed Delta table
Quality rules from the object's contract entry
processing: Run each declared rule against the landed data (e.g., not-null, row-count delta, uniqueness)
Aggregate rule results into a pass/fail evidence record
Attach the evidence record to this run's ledger entry
outputs: Quality evidence record tied to the run ID
Optional alert on rule failure
drill.example: The not_null(order_id) rule for 'returns' is evaluated against the newly landed rows; 3 violations are found and recorded as a failed-rule evidence entry on run 8472.
controls: Which rules block downstream consumption vs only warn
Evidence retention period
failureModes: Quality checks run after downstream consumers have already read the data, so a bad batch is discovered too late
A rule that should block the run is configured as warn-only and the bad data proceeds

nodes.label: Run ledger / state store
nodes.summary: Records what happened, and holds the watermark the next run needs.
nodes.detail: A persistent store of run history, itself typically a Delta table in OneLake: one entry per pipeline run instance, carrying status, rows processed, watermark position, and links to quality evidence and lineage. It is both the audit trail and the operational memory that makes the framework restartable rather than stateless.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the node that turns a series of independent runs into a framework: without it, every run starts from zero and 'incremental load' is impossible.

inputs: Run status from the pipeline run instance
Quality evidence record
New watermark position after successful write
processing: Write one ledger row per run: run ID, object, status, rows written, watermark, timestamp
On failure, retain the previous committed watermark rather than advancing it
Expose the latest committed watermark per object for the next run's config resolution
outputs: Watermark fed back into the next run's config resolution
Auditable run history for operations
drill.example: Run 8472 for 'returns' succeeds with 4,812 rows written; the ledger commits watermark updated_at=2026-07-12T00:00Z, which the next scheduled run will read as its starting point.
controls: What counts as 'success' for watermark advancement (all rules must pass vs write-only)
Retention/archival policy for old ledger entries
failureModes: A partially failed run advances the watermark anyway, silently skipping the unwritten rows on the next incremental pull
The ledger itself becomes a write bottleneck if every object's every run contends on the same table without partitioning

nodes.label: Lineage & telemetry
nodes.summary: Source-to-output lineage and monitoring signals captured for governance.
nodes.detail: Fabric's governance surface captures item-level metadata and lineage for the objects the framework touches, and monitoring hub / capacity metrics expose run-level operational signals. The framework should apply this at the same object boundary it uses for ownership, not as an afterthought bolted on separately.
nodes.whyItMatters: Lineage is what lets someone answer 'where did this number come from' months later; telemetry is what lets an operator see capacity strain before it becomes an incident.

evidence.note: Fabric's governance surface includes discovery/trust (OneLake catalog, lineage) and monitoring activity (monitoring hub, capacity metrics), and Purview Data Map can scan Fabric items to extract item-level metadata and lineage.

inputs: Run ledger entries
Item metadata from lakehouse tables touched by the run
processing: Scan/register item-level metadata and lineage edges (source object to target table) for the run's objects
Surface run-level operational metrics through the monitoring hub
outputs: Lineage graph entry linking source to 'returns' target table
Monitoring signal available in the admin monitoring workspace
drill.example: Purview Data Map records that lh_bronze.returns was last written by run 8472 of the metadata-driven pipeline, sourced from the 'returns' operational system.
controls: Scan frequency/scope for metadata scanning
Which monitoring signals trigger an alert
failureModes: Lineage capture lags actual writes, so an incident investigation sees a stale lineage graph
Monitoring is set up only at the pipeline level, missing capacity strain visible only at the object level

nodes.label: Metadata becomes a hidden language
nodes.summary: An over-flexible contract stops being config and starts being undocumented code.
nodes.detail: As more edge cases accumulate, teams add conditional flags, per-object overrides, and nested rule expressions directly into the metadata contract until interpreting an entry requires understanding a bespoke, undocumented execution model — the contract has become a programming language with no compiler, type system, or review discipline.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the most common way metadata-driven frameworks fail in practice: the framework's own flexibility becomes its biggest liability, and the failure mode is invisible until someone has to change it under pressure.

inputs: Metadata contract, after many incremental exception additions
processing: Each new edge case is solved by adding another conditional field to the contract rather than extending the executor
No schema versioning discipline is applied to the growing set of fields
New team members can no longer predict run behavior by reading the contract alone
outputs: A contract that requires reading pipeline/notebook code to interpret, defeating the purpose of externalizing configuration
drill.example: A single object's contract entry grows to include seven boolean override flags and two nested rule blocks that only the original author fully understands, and onboarding a new engineer now requires a code walkthrough rather than reading the metadata.
controls: A schema review gate before new contract fields are accepted
A cap or review trigger on per-object override count
failureModes: The framework becomes harder to change than the one-off pipelines it replaced
Silent behavior differences between objects because flags interact in ways no one tested

nodes.label: Non-idempotent retry corrupts data
nodes.summary: Retrying a failed write without watermark discipline duplicates or corrupts committed rows.
nodes.detail: If a pipeline activity's write is not idempotent (e.g., a blind append rather than a merge keyed on a natural key, or a write that ignores the ledger's last committed watermark), retrying a failed or partial run reprocesses rows that already landed, producing duplicates or inconsistent aggregates downstream.
nodes.whyItMatters: Retries are the normal recovery path in any orchestrated system; a framework that cannot retry safely turns every transient failure into a manual data-fix incident.

inputs: A partially completed run (e.g., 60% of rows written before failure)
A retry trigger (automatic or manual)
processing: Retry re-executes the same activity from the start rather than from the ledger's last confirmed watermark
The write step appends rather than merges, so already-landed rows are written a second time
outputs: Duplicate rows in the target Delta table
Downstream aggregates silently inflated
drill.example: A run for 'returns' fails after writing 3,000 of 4,812 rows; an automatic retry re-runs the full window and appends all 4,812 rows again, leaving 3,000 duplicates in the bronze table.
controls: Write strategy: merge/upsert on a natural key instead of blind append
Retry logic that resumes from the ledger's last committed watermark, not from the trigger's original window
failureModes: Downstream reports show inflated totals until someone manually de-duplicates the table
The duplication is discovered only when a business user questions a number, long after the retry happened

walkthrough.title: Start with the contract
walkthrough.explanation: Everything in the framework traces back to this versioned record of what data objects exist, where they come from, and what 'correct' means for each.

walkthrough.title: Resolve one object's run
walkthrough.explanation: The generic contract, combined with the last watermark, becomes a concrete parameter set for a single object's run — this is the translation step.

walkthrough.title: One pipeline, many objects
walkthrough.explanation: A single reusable Data Factory pipeline accepts those parameters instead of a bespoke pipeline existing per source — this is the reuse the pattern is built for.

walkthrough.title: Each trigger is its own run
walkthrough.explanation: Fabric tracks each execution as an independent run instance, which is what makes per-object retry and monitoring possible.

walkthrough.title: Transform logic is shared too
walkthrough.explanation: The pipeline invokes one reusable notebook for object-specific transform logic, parameterized the same way — reuse has to extend past the pipeline layer or the config-explosion risk just moves one layer down.

walkthrough.title: Data lands and self-registers
walkthrough.explanation: Fabric auto-validates and registers the Delta table in the metastore, so it's queryable immediately — but also immediately visible to consumers if the write is wrong.

walkthrough.title: Prove it's correct, not just that it ran
walkthrough.explanation: Contract-defined rules are evaluated against the landed data and recorded as evidence, separating 'the load succeeded' from 'the data is correct'.

walkthrough.title: The ledger is the framework's memory
walkthrough.explanation: Status, rows, and watermark are recorded here — this is what makes the next run incremental instead of starting from zero.

walkthrough.title: Governance catches up automatically
walkthrough.explanation: Lineage and monitoring signals are captured at the same object boundary as ownership, so the framework stays auditable as it scales.

walkthrough.title: The ledger closes the loop
walkthrough.explanation: The ledger's watermark feeds back into the next run's config resolution — without this feedback loop, this is just a batch job, not a metadata-driven framework.

walkthrough.title: Watch the contract's complexity
walkthrough.explanation: Left ungoverned, the contract accumulates conditional logic until it is an undocumented programming language only its author understands.

walkthrough.title: Retries must be safe
walkthrough.explanation: A blind retry on a non-idempotent write duplicates already-committed rows — recovery has to respect the ledger's watermark, not just re-run the trigger.
